reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: The chapter promises three things: what a terminal adds, who bears offline losses, and how to test a 'unified' claim

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Three key claims: the terminal is a computer that decides fraud liability, an offline payment is merchant credit, and 'unified commerce' is three separate checks

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Three failure patterns the chapter covers: offline approvals no issuer saw, counter refunds that cannot find the online payment, and dependence on one provider

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: An offline terminal still prints 'approved', raising the question of who approved and who pays

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A terminal is not a mere input device but a computer whose reading, offline storage and missing channel joins all cost the merchant

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The book's running €120 payment was made online, and this chapter covers the counter step it skipped

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Roadmap of the chapter's sections, ending with a side-by-side of Part II's six layers

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Two Requests From the Front Desk ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's 2,100 studios all use Adyen terminals, which carry about a fifth of member payments

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: Two Requests From the Front Desk ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Two requests the online stack could not answer: keep the terminal working without Wi-Fi, and refund an app purchase at the counter

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A magnetic stripe holds static data, so a copy is an indistinguishable counterfeit card

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The EMV chip produces a one-time cryptogram per transaction and is now near-universal / EMVCo publishes the standard but does not enforce it, so the rules with consequences belong to someone else

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The cryptogram only helps if the chip data travels intact through provider, acquirer and network to the issuer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Visa's EMV liability shift lets an issuer dispute counterfeit fraud when the chip was not read or the acquirer did not transmit full chip data

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Liability therefore depends on chip data surviving transit, so a certified terminal is useless if the provider drops the data (Visa only; Mastercard unverified)

reverse_outline.draft_locator: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A terminal is certified hardware with an expiring certification version and software the provider updates and restarts

reverse_outline.draft_locator: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Both providers encrypt card data by default and offer validated P2PE as an option, which determines the merchant's PCI questionnaire

reverse_outline.draft_locator: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Tap to pay on a phone replaces only the hardware; the provider, acquirer and certification remain, and certification may not cover every feature

reverse_outline.draft_locator: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen documents staged rollouts and Stripe only update mechanics, neither documents key loading or failure rates, so the deployer must keep its own per-device inventory

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Driving the Terminal: Local or Cloud, SDK or Server ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Till and terminal need a control channel carrying amounts and results but no card numbers, placed either in the store network or the provider's cloud

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Driving the Terminal: Local or Cloud, SDK or Server ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen's Terminal API follows the retail nexo protocol and runs either locally to the terminal's IP or through Adyen's cloud

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Driving the Terminal: Local or Cloud, SDK or Server ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe offers the same two placements as SDK and server-driven integrations, but built on its online PaymentIntent object

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Driving the Terminal: Local or Cloud, SDK or Server ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The four integration shapes pair up: in-store ones survive a connection drop at the cost of network work, cloud ones are simpler and stop with the link

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Driving the Terminal: Local or Cloud, SDK or Server ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Author's rule: cloud for many small unmanaged sites, in-store where selling through an outage matters more than network cost

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Meanings of Offline, and Who Carries the Loss ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The first meaning of offline is offline EMV, where the card approves on terms the issuer preset, and few debit cards support it

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Meanings of Offline, and Who Carries the Loss ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The second meaning is store-and-forward, where the terminal approves unverified and the merchant, as both providers state, carries the loss

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Meanings of Offline, and Who Carries the Loss ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The merchant's offline exposure is bounded by limits, which Adyen leaves to the merchant and Stripe caps itself with stricter entry rules

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Meanings of Offline, and Who Carries the Loss ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Store-and-forward only covers the shop's own connection failing, not a provider outage, and at Stripe must be prepared while online

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Meanings of Offline, and Who Carries the Loss ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: A stored payment gets its platform reference and its real outcome later, so the late result needs its own path into the merchant's records

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Unified Commerce Is Three Separate Checks ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Providers advertise 'unified commerce' without defining it; the author splits it into three separable properties to verify one by one

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Unified Commerce Is Three Separate Checks ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Check one, a shared payer identifier: both providers can recognise a card across channels, but recognising and charging are different objects and phone wallets break the match

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Unified Commerce Is Three Separate Checks ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Check two, a cross-channel refund: at both providers it works only when the till can supply the original payment's reference

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Unified Commerce Is Three Separate Checks ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Check three, one settlement report for both channels: the documentation gives no field-level proof, so test real files, especially for stored offline payments

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Unified Commerce Is Three Separate Checks ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Each of the three checks has its own test and failure mode, so passing one says nothing about the others

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen publishes in-person volumes and terminal counts while Stripe publishes none, so the two cannot be ranked on scale

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: A table sets out seven consistent differences between Stripe and Adyen, with the author's reading as inference

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Advice per provider: on Stripe design around the PaymentIntent and decide on offline early; on Adyen pick local or cloud and own limits, references and certificates

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Estate, No Offline, Three Checks ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield chose a single terminal provider to avoid duplicating the device estate, certification and adapter for a low-margin channel

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Estate, No Offline, Three Checks ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield refused offline acceptance because its cloud integration and online-dependent till make it useless / the declined exposure would have been about €3,000 per terminal per outage, a credit limit needing an owner

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Estate, No Offline, Three Checks ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: At studios split across Stripe and Adyen none of the three checks passes at provider level, so Larkfield supplies identifier, refund path and reconciliation itself

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Estate, No Offline, Three Checks ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Even with both channels on Adyen, a counter refund of an online payment depends on a lookup in Larkfield's own payment record

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Failure: the till loses the terminal mid-payment, and retrying without checking status double-charges the customer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Failure: a stored payment is declined after the customer left, and without an owner for the write-off it stays 'paid' in the till

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Failure: terminals silently fall out of service through certification, staleness or relocation, visible only in a device inventory

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Failure: a provider outage stops a single-provider counter, a risk Larkfield accepts by falling back to cash or the app

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Established facts: the chip's one-time cryptogram, Visa's counterfeit liability rule, and the two offline mechanisms with merchant liability for store-and-forward

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Context-dependent choices: local versus cloud, whether to accept offline, and one provider versus two across channels

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Author's synthesis: treat a terminal rollout as taking on a device estate and a credit line, and test 'unified' as three separate checks including a phone wallet

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The terminal is the last of six differently owned layers around the issuer's decision, so an approval rate belongs to a whole stack and does not transfer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield keeps two providers with a rehearsed switch instead of an orchestration layer because the value is in knowing each stack / the opening queue's answer is that nobody had approved and the studio was the lender / a short list of what to record per provider, country and counter

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Nine questions a team should ask about chip data, device inventory, outages, offline credit, forwarded outcomes, card recognition, cross-channel refunds, settlement reports and unknown outcomes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: An approval is not yet money: it creates debts settled over days that need a second record, which Part III takes up

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.draft_locus: In Practice at Larkfield: One Estate, No Offline, Three Checks ¶2
results.quote: Femke still sized what was being declined: a store-and-forward maximum of €120 (one ten-class pass) and 25 stored payments per terminal *(assumption)* would cap the exposure at 25 × €120 = **€3,000 per terminal per outage**. That is a credit limit, and it needs an owner before it needs a configuration screen.
results.finding: The paragraph gives the reasons for refusing offline acceptance and then a second point with its own conclusion: the size of the exposure as a credit limit that needs an owner. The reverse outliner needed two phrases. The spec puts both in p35 (the sizing is an evidence item whose 'shows' is a different idea from the controlling idea), so the draft cannot separate them without adding a unit.

results.draft_locus: What to Take Away ¶5
results.quote: As for the queue on that Saturday morning: nobody had approved those payments yet, and the studio was the lender. What to write down, for each provider and country, is short:
results.finding: The paragraph justifies Larkfield's K8, describes the 1,140 split studios, answers the opening question and lists what to write down; the reverse outliner needed three phrases. The spec's controlling idea for p46 is itself compound and the conclusion's callback and takeaway are both assigned to this one unit.

results.draft_locus: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶2
results.quote: EMVCo's statistics, measured on card-present transactions over the twelve months to the fourth quarter of 2025, put chip at "97% of card-based transactions" worldwide.
results.finding: The statistic is given and the paragraph moves straight to another EMVCo statement; no sentence says what the 97% shows (the spec: chip is the normal case, so the exceptions are what an architect must look for).

results.draft_locus: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶1
results.quote: A payment terminal is a certified computer with an expiry date.
results.finding: Boundary from 'What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶5' into this section. The spec declares cause_effect, carrying over that liability depends on what the terminal reads and what is transmitted. The section opens with a new claim and no link to the liability rule; both flow readers said the reason the section comes here is not stated and had to be inferred.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶1
results.quote: **The outcome is unknown at the till.** The till loses contact with the terminal after the card was presented, and the customer may or may not have been charged.
results.finding: Boundary from 'In Practice at Larkfield: One Estate, No Offline, Three Checks ¶4' into this section. The spec declares a contrast in one sentence, carrying over Larkfield's decisions when everything works and introducing the failures they must survive. The section starts with the first failure; no sentence expresses the contrast or picks up Larkfield's decisions.

results.draft_locus: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶3
results.quote: Adyen (May 2026) says store-and-forward in its Mobile SDK for Android is in limited availability "because it is not yet PCI MPoC certified".
results.finding: 'Store-and-forward' is used as a known term two sections before it is named and explained in the offline section; at this point the reader does not know what is in limited availability.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item A1; flow reader B, item B8

results.draft_locus: A Terminal Is a Managed Computer ¶2
results.quote: Adyen (2025) says its default needs only "the SAQ B-IP", with the caveat that E2EE "does not have the PCI P2PE-validated “stamp”"; Stripe (n.d., accessed November 2026) says "Stripe P2PE is an optional, paid feature" and that Terminal-only merchants "can validate using SAQ C".
results.finding: 'SAQ B-IP' and 'SAQ C' are named without saying what distinguishes them, so the reader cannot tell whether the two providers differ or which questionnaire is lighter; 'Terminal-only' uses Stripe's product name before the product is introduced, and 'scope' is sent to another chapter unexplained.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item A2; flow reader B, item B7

results.draft_locus: What the Chip Adds, and Who Pays When It Is Not Read ¶4
results.quote: It works through disputes ([[refunds-reversals-and-disputes]]) and is not a law.
results.finding: After the aside on 3-D Secure, 'It' first reads as 3-D Secure and the reader has to go back to see it means the liability shift; the Visa sentence that follows strings seven quoted fragments and needed a second reading to separate the conditions.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, items A3 and A4; flow reader B, items B4 and B5

results.draft_locus: What to Take Away ¶5
results.quote: That is why Larkfield's K8 keeps two providers and one rehearsed switch and adds no orchestration product: at its volume the gain is in knowing each stack, and a routing layer would unify the request while leaving two sets of disputes, settlements and stored cards.
results.finding: Both readers lost the thread most here: 'That is why' has no clear referent in the six-layer table before it, and the paragraph then does three more jobs in a row, so the answer to the chapter's opening question is buried in the middle. The jobs and their order are the spec's (p46 holds the K8 consequence, the callback and the takeaway).

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶1
results.quote: The terminal on the counter still lights up when a card is tapped and still prints "approved".
